messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Valentina Reyes is a 24-year-old Salvadoran American woman who works the day shift at a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city. She came to the intake appointment wearing a grey hoodie pulled low, and she spent much of the first session with her gaze directed at the floor or the middle distance — rarely, and only briefly, meeting the clinician's eyes. She described herself as someone who used to be social, someone her coworkers called *la que siempre ríe*, the one who always laughs. That version of herself, she said quietly, felt like a stranger now.

Fourteen months ago, Valentina was present during a pipe-bomb detonation at an outdoor community festival in her neighborhood — an event she had attended every summer since childhood. She had been standing near a food stall when the device exploded approximately thirty feet away. The blast threw her off her feet. In the seconds that followed, there was smoke, screaming, and a confusion of bodies moving in every direction. She recalls the smell of burning and the sight of a man near her falling, and then — nothing. A gap. She does not know how she got from the ground to the far side of a chain-link fence, nor what she did in the minutes between the explosion and the arrival of emergency services. No matter how many times she has tried to reconstruct that interval, the memory simply is not there, and its absence frightens her in a way she finds difficult to articulate. She knows what happened — a bomb went off, people were hurt, she survived — but when she tries to put the experience into language, the words dissolve before she can reach them. She has attempted to write about it twice and abandoned the page both times.

In the weeks after the attack, Valentina returned to the warehouse because she needed the income. The warehouse floor became the first place where her changed nervous system made itself known in daily life. The facility is enormous and loud: forklifts reverse with warning beeps, pallets drop from height, coworkers shout across aisles. Any sudden movement in her peripheral vision — a colleague stepping quickly around a corner, a hand raised to gesture — sends a jolt through her body that she cannot suppress. She has come to believe that her body is no longer reliable, that it responds to the world according to its own rules rather than hers, and this loss of confidence in her own physical self has been quietly humiliating. A supervisor once asked why she flinched when he tapped her shoulder, and she had no answer she was willing to give.

Valentina has developed a habit of arriving at her shift early enough to walk the warehouse floor before others fill it, mapping the space so that nothing will surprise her. She positions herself during breaks with her back to the wall. At night, in her apartment, she finds it nearly impossible to feel safe — the darkness seems to carry a quality of exposure that daylight does not, and she often lies awake running through sounds she cannot identify. She scans constantly: doorways, windows, the street below. She had come to believe, in a way that felt less like a thought and more like a fact, that the world is a dangerous place and that she is the only one paying sufficient attention to it.

When memories of the festival surface without warning, what rises with them is not grief or fear but a rage so sudden and consuming that it alarms her. She has learned to manage this by going somewhere private and doing what she describes as "leaving" — deliberately detaching from her body, going blank, waiting for the feeling to pass. It works, after a fashion, but she loses time, and afterward she feels hollowed out.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a conversation with her younger sister, who told her she had stopped seeming like herself. Valentina had not realised how visible the change had become. She came to the first session hoping, in her words, to "get back inside my own body." What she fears most is that the version of herself she is hoping to recover no longer exists.
